name: Jheri curl

card.summary: A chemical curl treatment that turns tight textured hair into loose, glossy curls, giving a wet-look, defined hairstyle.
card.aka: Jheri Curl, curly perm, wet look
card.note: Chemical processing can leave hair dry and brittle; activator products have been linked to flammability burns.

quick.overview:
The Jheri curl is a permanent-wave hairstyle that became popular among Black Americans in the 1980s. It loosens tight curls and resets them into soft, shiny curls rather than straightening them, giving the hair a glossy, defined look.

It is named for chemist Jheri Redding. Comer Cottrell's at-home Curly Kit helped it spread, and wearers included Michael Jackson, Eazy-E and Ice Cube.
quick.how: A two-step chemical process: a softening cream containing ammonium thioglycolate loosens the natural curl, the hair is set on perm rods, and a neutraliser fixes the new shape. Daily upkeep uses curl activator and moisturiser, and wearers often sleep under a plastic cap.
quick.risks: The chemicals can leave natural hair brittle and dry, and activator is greasy and can stain fabrics. A 1988 Detroit burn-unit review reported 12 patients burned after accidentally igniting a hair activator product.

lead: The Jheri curl is a permanent-wave hairstyle that was popular among Black Americans and other Black communities in the 1980s and early 1990s, giving hair a glossy, loosely curled look instead of a fully straight one [2]. It is credited to chemist Jheri Redding, and entrepreneur Comer Cottrell later introduced an at-home Curly Kit so people could copy the style without salon prices [2][3].

The look is produced in two steps: a rearranging cream with ammonium thioglycolate loosens the natural curl, the hair is set on rods, and a neutraliser such as an oxidising agent permanently curls it. Daily upkeep with curl activator and moisturiser keeps the sheen [2].

Wearers have included Michael Jackson, Edmund Sylvers, Eazy-E and Ice Cube, and the style was parodied in films and television in the late 1980s [2]. One case series from the Detroit Medical Center recorded facial and scalp burns from accidentally igniting activator product [1].

A polished, wet-look hairstyle with daily activator upkeep
angle.text: The treatment directly changes the texture of the hair into loose, shiny curls that wearers maintain with daily moisturising products. It is a style choice that was fashionable in the 1980s.

infobox: Jheri Redding; at-home kit by Comer Cottrell

paras: A softening cream with ammonium thioglycolate loosens the natural curl. The loosened hair is set on perm rods and a neutraliser, usually an oxidising agent, fixes the curl [2].
Wearers apply curl activator and moisturiser daily and sleep under plastic caps. Activator is greasy and can stain clothing and furniture, and regrowth requires touch-ups [2].

Grokipedia attributes the style to Jheri Redding in the late 1970s and says Comer Cottrell's Pro-Line Curly Kit, introduced in 1979, put it within reach of home users [3]. Michael Jackson wore it on Thriller, and films such as Coming to America and Pulp Fiction depicted or referenced it [2][3].

A review of 1,008 admissions to the Detroit Medical Center Burn Unit found 12 patients burned by accidentally igniting a hair activator product called Jheri-Curl; eleven were superficial partial-thickness burns and one needed skin grafting [1]. The chemicals can also leave hair brittle and dry [2].
No studies found on the hairstyle's effects beyond the burn-unit case series described above [1].

timeline.event: Pro-Line's Curly Kit brings the style to home users [3].
Detroit burn-unit series reports activator ignition burns [1].
